spellchecked: CALIFORNIA INTELLIGENCE. The Alta California of the 15th April gives the following summary of recent events on the Pacific side of the Union. Since our last steamer paper, the most important event in California has been the repeal by the Legislature of the odious and disastrous foreign miners tax bill of last year and proclamation to that effect by our Governor. The health of this city has been remarkably good and the same may be asserted of the entire State for at least any reports have been received. There can be no healthier country in the world than California. The annals of crime are about as dark as ever, but the chances of punishment seem to have improved thereby. The two men, Worden and Stuart, indicted for the murder and robbery of Mr. Janson and whose supposed guilt had nearly been expiated by Lynch law, have been tried before the district court and found guilty of assault with intent to kill and robbery. The jury sentenced Stuart to fourteen years in the penitentiary, the utmost they could give him. He has since been taken to Yuba County, to be tried for murder. Worden was sentenced to ten years in the penitentiary. The Legislature passed a bill authorizing the Attorney General to enter nolle prosequi in the case of Charles Robinson and others of Sacramento indicted for conspiracy and murder in the squatter case, which has been vetoed by the Governor. There has been a fight in Sonora growing out of some conflicting miner claims in which one man, by the name of Davis, was killed and several others wounded. It was rumored that five men had been killed, which proved false. The great fire at Nevada city was not as destructive to property as was at first reported. Forty thousand dollars in loss is said will cover the loss, which was at first placed at one hundred thousand dollars. Governor McDougal has been appealed to for his aid in suppressing the Indian depredations in the Mariposa region and the Legislature responded to his call upon them by granting him authority to call five hundred men for that purpose. Taking a tour for the purpose of acquiring information upon the subject, he reached the conclusion that they were not needed and has not called them into service. One of the Indian Commissioners has recently been in this city, bringing some of the friendly chiefs with him, and reports rather favorably of the chances of forming treaties with the tribes in the vicinity of the Merced, Mariposa, and Fresno Buttes. Certain tribes will have to be soundly dubbed before they will enter into treaties or keep them when formed. McCauley, indicted for the murder of Judge Sellers in Napa City, has been tried, found guilty, and sentenced to be hung on the 14th of this month. No small degree of pleasure and surprise has been felt here by the arrival of the clipper ship SURPRISE from New York, in ninety-six days and fifteen hours, the shortest on record. During the past month of March, the snow has appeared in the mountains beyond the San Jose valley and further to the north. This rain will prove of inestimable value to the agricultural interests of the State and perhaps to many of the miners. The trial of Charles Duane for assault with intent to kill Amede Fayo has terminated in the jury agreeing and Duane has been admitted to bail in the sum of five thousand dollars. Several hundred thousand dollars of redeemed city scrip has been burnt by our council. Intelligence from many points in the mines is more cheering than hitherto during the winter. The Commissioners appointed by the Legislature to select the public lands to be donated by Gen. Vallejo to the State as sites for public buildings, have attended to their duties, returned, and reported to the Legislature, and now we suppose the work of erecting the various buildings, offices, etc., at Vallejo will commence. The prospects of this season agriculturally are, we believe, very promising. FROM THE MINING DISTRICTS. The Alta California says that the news from the Gold Bluff is very favorable, a rich lead of gold has been discovered there from which one machine washed over thirty-two ounces of gold in a day. On another day, seventy-two hundred dollars were taken out. The gold is found upon the bedrock from two to ten feet below the surface. One bucket of dirt yielded eight ounces, ten pounds had been taken from twenty pounds of the surface sand, an average of six dollars the pound. The Warren, which arrived from the locality of San Francisco on the 29th of March, brought twenty thousand dollars in gold. The San Francisco STANDARD of April says: 'We continue to receive cheering news from all portions of the gold region. The Cosumnes, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Mokelumne, American, Feather, Scott, Klamath, and other rivers in the gold mining country send favorable accounts. The latest from the region of San Diego makes it certain that valuable deposits of the golden mineral have been discovered there by the Mexicans, and reports from the adjacent portions of the State render it probable that the mines there will be found much more productive than it was supposed they would be.' One of the dredging companies, to which we have heretofore referred, preparing to operate has just got to work. During the week just past, the dredging steamboat Phoenix set to work for the purpose of testing the capabilities of the machinery and the richness of the bed of the river at that point and the results of the experiment yielded several nugget quantities per hour. The quartz mining operations have also been prosecuted with vigor and success. Some of the veins are rich beyond all previous calculations. Here are one or two instances of a very common mode of administering justice in criminal cases in our midst. A drunken Englishman, named Diggie, murdered his wife under circumstances of unusual cruelty. During their whole residence in Georgetown, she had supported him and their children by her own industry. He asked her one morning for some money to gamble with, but she told him to wait until he was sober. He rushed across the room for a pistol, but she anticipated him and threw it in a bucket of water. He then leaped into the streetes, snatched a rifle from the shoulder of a passer-by, returned and shot her through the heart. It was Sunday, and as usual the places of resort were filled by miners, who invariably spend that holiday in town. The report of a rifle in the street was nothing unusual but the tale of horror flew as only rumor can fly, and in five minutes the house was filled. In such country as ours, and under such circumstances as these, men act rather than speak. A neighboring 'Round Tent' (our gambling houses are often turned into courtrooms on account of their size) was selected as the scene of trial. The prisoner was led in and then, before a word was spoken, another party brought in the body of his wife, just as she fell, with the dark blood oozing from her breast. She was gently laid on a large table near her husband. This sight stung the people into frenzy. No one thought of wasting words in trial. The prisoner was seized, and hurried towards a little eminence overlooking the village, where the noose of a lariat swung significantly from a tree. Just at this moment, a man of great influence with the people of that vicinity attempted to persuade them to postpone their design until a Coroner's inquest should be held upon the body and a summary trial, but still a trial, had after their verdict. With much difficulty he succeeded on condition that the inquest be held upon that day; and, as the Coroner was at Coloma, four o'clock was given as the last moment. An express was sent to Coloma, and, to save time, a jury was empaneled to act instantly upon his arrival. They sat together in the tent with the prisoner and the body. The mob waited outside but were not unemployed. A deep pit was dug at the foot of the tree, and all the solemn furniture of the grave prepared. As four o'clock approached, the silence of the mob was broken by deep whispers and hoarse murmurs. Rifles, pistols, and bowie knives were freely displayed. This did not escape the notice of the jury, and they began, not unnaturally, to fear for their own safety. At last, when the sun was low in the west, the mob could wait no longer but tore up the sides of the tent and rushed in, just in time to see the last juryman escaping by a back way. They went at their task without a word. At the head of a long procession, the murderer marched to his gallows and the body of his wife was borne close behind him. The children, thank Heaven!, were not there forgotten. A small box, marked 'For the Orphans,' was nailed to the tree, and many an ounce was poured into it from the purses of those who followed the father to his death. The body of the murdered woman was lowered into a wide pit and even while the wretched man gazed upon it, and upon that empty but significant box by his side the cord suddenly tightened around his neck and his spirit was dispatched to the eternal. The mob sat at the hillside and sternly watched him. At the end of half an hour, he was cut down and laid near the body of his wife. In five minutes Georgetown was as still as that lonely grave upon the hill. Not a man was to be seen in the streets; no one knew anything of that lawless mob. In the evening, the Coroner arrived, and upon hearing the story, summoned his jury for the morning. They met upon the hill and stood around the unified grave, while the end of a cut cord dangled above their heads. They exchanged a few words, and after laying a slip of paper upon each of the bodies, proceeded to fill up the grave. Upon one of the slips was written 'Murdered by Divine, her husband' and on the other 'Died according to the will of God by the justice of men'. Yesterday evening, Dr. Lennox, from Scotland, was shot while sitting in his office. This morning, the man who had often menaced his life, was seized on suspicion, and examined before the proper authorities. Everyone rushed out. The Sheriff calling all lovers of law and order to his assistance attempted a recapture. He was backed by a large party, but many ran to the other side. There is no mistaking this general public feeling of indignation. The participants in this exciting affair are not rowdies, but the majority of our best citizens. The feeling of insecurity is entertained by a feeling that the laws afford no protection and a determination to take matters into their own hands and make an example. Let nothing be done rashly let satisfactory proof be given of guilt before punishment is executed, for the bitterest that the heart could bear in future life would be the remembrance that through the instrumentality of any one innocent had been consigned to an ignominious and violent death. As an example of public feeling, I publish the following notice, which was in circulation in the form of handbill yesterday: 'Citizens of San Francisco.-The series of murders and robberies that have been committed in this city, without the least redress from the laws leave us entirely in a state of anarchy. When thieves are left without control to rob and kill then doth the honest traveler fear each bush thief. The law appears, is but nonentity to be scoffed at. Redress can no longer be had for aggression but through the quick remedy admirably laid down in the code of Judge Lynch. Not that one should admire this process for redress but that we are assassinated in our domiciles and the law seems to let our aggressors perambulate the merely because they have furnished straw bail. About dusk, a much larger crowd gathered around the City Hall and organized themselves into a meeting, appointing Wm. D. M. Howard, Esq. President. The meeting was addressed by Judge Tilford, Judge Morse, Mayor Geary, Samuel Brannan, Esq., and others. In the noise and confusion that existed, a committee of twelve was finally appointed to consult with the authorities and guard and protect the prisoners till ten o'clock today. Mr. Brannan then addressed the people, and told them that if the committee of which Mr. Brannan was a member) did not deliver up these prisoners at ten o'clock today they might hang him. After the appointment of the committee, the greater portion of the crowd dispersed and the committee remained in the clerk's office of the Recorder's court. The Alta California of the next day continues the recital as follows: Yesterday morning, at ten o'clock a large concourse of people had gathered around the courthouse for the purpose of receiving the report of the committee who had been appointed the night previous. Mr. Brannan from the committee reported to the citizens that the prisoners were safe and asked that the prisoners might be discharged which was done. Remarks were then made by Mayor Geary Judge Parsons Judge Tilford and others all of whom urged the propriety of calm and cool action, and of the trial of Wildyed and Stuart by the proper authorities which sentiment appeared to meet with general consent. By eleven o'clock the crowd gathered around the courthouse must have amounted to six thousand people, who were as orderly and quiet as so large a body can be. Mayor Geary proposed that a committee of twelve citizens be appointed to sit with the examining justice tomorrow as a jury, and that their verdict be final. This was negatived, and it was resolved to proceed to the trial forthwith. Judge and jury, clerk and sheriff were appointed and after a long examination and labored argument on both sides, retired and after considerable deliberation reported that they stood nine for conviction and three in doubt of the identity of the accused. The tumult was very great during the absence of the jury from the courtroom. Judge Spence, Mr. Coleman, and others, addressed the multitude. At midnight the crowd had somewhat abated, and a number disposed to adopt the recommendation of the Judge.

The man described received the commission as Consul to Lyons, France, a city containing a population of some 100,000, and continued intercourse with this country, both in trade commerce and immigration. That such specimen of willigery should be the Representative of this government in such a city is among the mysteries of refined Taylorism. That paper thus describes the Consul: What on earth could have induced General Taylor to select such vulgar specimen of humanity as Heudebert, our Consul at the refined city of Lyons, we cannot imagine. Surely he did not know the character of the man who, if sent anywhere at all, should be sent to the Penitentiary as nuisance and curse to society. Some years ago, Heudebert was citizen of this city, where he kept an eating house. With his career in this city we are uninformed, but informed that it was of such a character as to render him odious. He was compelled to remove his culinary utensils and kitchen furniture to another place. After much trouble, he succeeded in getting possession of the Race Course in Jefferson County, known as 'Hamlin's track,' where he kept a doggery and gambling house. Mr. Hamlin, who resides near the track, soon became disgusted with his conduct, and one day told him he must keep a decent house, or he would be compelled to turn him out of it. Not being able to comply with this very proper demand, Heudebert removed his various implements of trade to Port Gibson. What kind of establishment he kept at Port Gibson, we do not know, nor do we know how long he resided there, but we know he was ordered to leave on account of his vulgarities and insult to a very respectable lady. In fact, such was the nature of his offense, that he barely escaped the penalties of Lynch Law. When we heard of Heudebert again, he had opened a grocery and gambling house in Jackson. With his career in Jackson well acquainted. He has been several times indicted for keeping gambling and disorderly house, and at one time he was informed by several respectable heads of families, that if he did not stop his Keno table, they would drive him as nuisance from the city, and throw his gambling cards and apparatus into Pearl River. This was a heavy blow to his prospects. 'By golly, gentlemen,' said the horror-stricken Heudebert, 'just as I begin to make my fortune, by innocent amusement, you tell me I must leave your damned town; you in Natchy, you win my money at the Hamberlin tract--you drive me to Jackson, and now you tell me I must go some other place, or you will throw all my things into the Pearl River. I have one damn hard time of it. I do not ask your boys to play Keno. Sometimes they win, sometimes they lose. I do not ask them to drink, but they be good customers, for they drink when they be dry, and when they are asked, always. Ah, gentlemen, this country is not longer free, and I shall cry very much.' The planking of the Detroit and Howell road is rapidly progressing. Already the plank is down several miles and gate erected. This road is one of the greatest thoroughfares in the State and will be made still greater by the planking of it. It will enable farmers to get into market at all of the year, with double the loads that they have heretofore been able to draw. The Detroit and Birmingham plank road is also rapidly progressing. One mile of the plank is already down, and the work of grading and placing plank on the line is going forward rapidly. This is the thoroughfare in the State. Even in these dull times teams are continually passing to and from the city over the road. The city is destined to reap a rich harvest by means of these roads. Plank roads make business. Every good farmer keeps a team, and with good roads and low toll at all seasons, a vast amount of produce, wood, etc., will be brought to market by those who have not been able to do so heretofore. This will create greater competition in the market, and enable all to purchase the necessaries much cheaper. At the same time, the profits of the producer will be increased from the fact that larger loads be drawn and teams turned to better account. We hope to see the charters granted in 1848 in various parts of the State, taken, and the work commenced. The stock will not only be good, but the increased facilities to farmers will tend to open and settle the unoccupied lands. Every farmer who has any spare means should be a stockholder in the road which is nearest to his farm. spellchecked: A SERIOUS AFFAIR.--We are informed that, on Sunday evening last, in Illinoistown, opposite this city, two men, coopers by trade, in a drunken frolic, went in a house where they insulted some ladies. One of the men was named John Hamer, a German, and the other John Ray, an Englishman. The owner of the house soon returned, and finding what had been done, commenced an assault upon them, and beat them severely with a hoop pole. The two fled to their boarding house. Subsequently, a number of persons assembled and went to the tavern where Hamer and Ray were in bed, took them out, and after severely lynching them, put them into a skiff and sent them over to this city. It is said that the skiff was bored full of holes, and that they only gave them a couple of sticks to work their way over on this side. The Irishman, Ray, having made the most resistance, was worse beaten than Hamer. They succeeded in reaching this side, and since then, Ray has died of the injuries received. Yesterday Hamer was taken to Belleville, to institute proceedings against the parties engaged in the mob. Ray is represented as a man of considerable property here, in Peoria, and in Cincinnati, Ohio. In the latter place, he is said to have a family. A considerable sum in gold, and a number of deeds and other papers, left by him, are in the possession of the keeper of the hotel in Illinoistown, where he was staying. The subject, we are assured, will undergo medical investigation. St. Louis Republican

On the 18th inst., a serious outrage resulting in murder occurred at Edwardsville, ILL. The St. Louis Republican says: James Duncan, a farmer, somewhat notorious as a quarrelsome and bad character, having some difficulty with those in the neighborhood, had been warned to leave, and threatened with death if he remained. Early yesterday morning he was informed that a large party was coming down, and was advised to leave, which he refused and prepared to defend himself. Accompanied by a woman who had lived with him, both armed with guns, they left the house to go fishing, when they met the party, some twenty or thirty in number, on their way to the house. As they approached, the woman discharged her gun in their midst, wounding one of the party very seriously, and immediately after a volley was returned by which Duncan was instantly killed, the top of his head being shot away and a large number of shots took effect in his body. The woman received a ball in her breast, from which it is supposed she cannot recover. Duncan had no family, and the woman was living with him as a housekeeper. COOL FORETHOUGHT The most admirable instance of prudential forethought we ever heard of occurred in Boston a few days since. Three Irishmen were engaged in taking down a wall in Mount Vernon Street. The wall fell upon and buried them. A lady from the opposite side of the street rushed out, and calling to those who were rescuing the poor fellows, said, 'Bring them in here. Bring them in here. I have everything ready. I have been expecting this all day.' The men were carried into her house, and true enough she had 'everything ready' bandage, lint, laudanum, and all. If this is not an instance of 'cool forethought' we know not what is. MORE OUTRAGES AGAINST THE MORMONS By the St. Croix, which arrived last evening from the upper Mississippi, says the St. Louis Reporter of the 19th instant, we have received a circular, issued at Nauvoo, July 10th, calling on the order loving citizens of Hancock to assemble and aid in suppressing, as far as possible, existing outbreaks against the Mormons remaining in the vicinity of Nauvoo, and those friendly to them. It would seem that, owing to the scarcity of farming hands in that neighborhood, few Mormons have been employed by the farmers in gathering their crops. This has given umbrage to the lynchers, who recently assembled in considerable force, and going to a harvest field where some six or eight persons were at work, some of them new citizens, inflicted summary and dreadful punishment on them all. We further learn from the clerk of the St. Croix, says the Reporter, that a party of some eighty men from Nauvoo had turned out, and captured five or six of the principal rioters. SHOCKING TRAGEDY We learn, says the St. Louis Organ, that a man by the name of James Duncan, who resided near Collinsville, ILL., when a short distance from his dwelling which he had just left in company with Miss Page, to go fishing, was attacked on the morning of the 18th by about forty armed men, some disguised, and shot by several of them. He was instantly killed, his body being perforated by thirty or forty bullets. Miss Page was wounded in the breast. She fought bravely, shooting and morally wounding one of the party. She afterwards fled to the woods, in her fright, and has not been seen since. The murderers all fled after committing their diabolical outrage, and no cause for the deed is known. A demand for his release was sent two days ago, which was refused. There are eight regular packet boats plying up the Illinois, making trip a week, and so arranged as to leave daily, Sundays excepted. On the Mississippi four packets making two trips per week to Keokuck, which is at the foot of the lower Rapids there besides 10 which run above Burlington, Bloomington, Galena and Dubuque, and as far up as St. Anthony Falls. The Missouri packets make their regular trips to Lexington, Independence and Weston. Occasionally a boat visits Council Bluffs and once year the American Fur Company sends a boat up to the Yellowstone, 2700 miles above us, with provisions for the companies and bring on their return, the result of their winters trappings. Had those who live IN the Eastern States an opportunity OF witnessing the hustle and activity on our eve, and the large stores upon Main, Market, Fourth, and other streets, they would not call it a benighted place. We know that the people of Lincoln County in this state have been much excited for some months past over the discovery of the existence of a band of counterfeiters and horse thieves among them. Several of them have been at different times arrested, and suspicion continued to rest against other families. In this state of tension, a company of Regulators was formed to order the suspected individuals to leave the county, failing to do which, summary punishment was inflicted. Two young men of the family named Turnbull fell under the suspicion of the Regulators and on Friday last were met at a house in the county to determine what should be done with them. It is not known what was agreed upon at that meeting, but from thence they proceeded to the residence of old Mr. Turnbull, father of the young men in question. The old man, who was at his shop, saw them approach and attempted to escape into the house but was intercepted and caught. Two younger and the females of the family retreated into the house and locked the doors. The suspected men were not to be found. The Lynchers surrounded the house for a time and finally set fire to it, but it was extinguished by the family. They then resolved upon more efficient measures and one of them seized a tool with which, after several blows, broke the door, and the mob entered. A general fight ensued. It is not known which party fired first, but two shots were fired by the young Turner, one of which killed a young man by the name of Davis. He died only twenty-four hours after the affray. Another of the mob, named Norrell or Norris, had been injured in the fracas, having received a wound in the head with a weapon resembling a corn knife, which penetrated into the skull and he is not expected to live long. A third was injured slightly. One of the Turnbulls was shot in the knee and was dying at the last accounts. The other was hit in the thigh and was not expected to survive. One young boy, about sixteen years old, was missing and unaccounted for. This occurred about eight miles back of Baileyville between 11 and 12 o'clock of the day. Great excitement followed throughout the county. The mob had determined on meeting on Monday to proceed to the Turnbull's house to exterminate the whole family, but it is hoped that the efforts being made to arrest this design will be successful. It is said that the Regulators are composed of some of the respectable citizens of the county, but how they can reconcile their proceedings with a desire to maintain this character is beyond our comprehension. St. Louis Republican.

spellchecked: The following sketch of Captain Rynders' life we have obtained from various authentic sources. It will be seen by it, that in him are found the elements which admirably qualify him for popular leader of the Don Giovanni school, bold, reckless and fearless with more wit than wisdom and more promptitude than prudence--ambitious of being a popular hero devoted to women, wine, and free living--fond of fun and fight and always ready to protect the women and the weak and defend the right against all odds. He was born in the village of Waterford, Saratoga County, New York, some thirty-eight winters ago. From the age of ten to the year 1832 Mr. Rynders operated upon the North River, first as hand, then as commander, when he got the title of captain, and lastly as owner of two vessels. During this period he sailed on several foreign voyages, to different parts of the world. In these voyages occurred many exciting incidents and thrilling adventures, which we have no room to relate. In 30, the year of the cholera while in the ownership and command of vessels upon the North River, Captain Rynders, through sundry bad debts and speculations upon the turf, to which he has always been slightly addicted, failed, as many distinguished individuals have done before and since. Unsuccessful in settling up his debts, and his creditors being inexorable, in Dec. 1832, Capt. Rynders sailed for New Orleans. As a specimen of incidents which chequered his life upon the ocean we may relate one or two adventures upon this passage to New Orleans, as given to us by a passenger and eyewitness. The captain of the packet was taken sick, and the whole duty devolved upon the mate. The crew became refractory, disobedient, and mutinous. Capt. Rynders saw the peril of the ship, and, at the risk of his life, took side with the mate, seized the helm, and by his boldness and decision, Red Rover-like quelled the mutiny, and restored order. By this coup de main, Capt Rynders saved the ship from the rocks, when she was fast driving, having been steered upon the wrong course, and all on board from shipwreck. The ship was afterwards chased by pirates, to the great horror and alarm of all on board, except our Don Giovanni. He resolved on flight, and to that end called all hands to quarters; mustered all the old swords, muskets, handspikes and implements of fight which could be found on board, and desperately resolved to repel boarders or die in the attempt. The pirate came alongside but on discovering the uncivil reception which they were likely to meet with, they very wisely concluded to keep out of mischief and hauled off. The commander of the vessel returned public thanks to Captain Rynders, restored to him his passage money, and expressed his lasting obligations to him for twice saving his ship. Within three weeks after his arrival in New Orleans, Captain Rynders became the hero of a popular row in front of the Camp Street Theatre. These were the days when the notorious pugilist O'Rourke was in his glory. On the evening in question, O'Rourke was to have a boxing match with a celebrated Englishman upon the boards of the theatre. The theatre was jammed inside and thousands were collected in front of it, chiefly Irish, and friends of O'Rourke. In the excitement report reached the crowd outside that O'Rourke was getting whipped by the Englishman. The Irish were roused to frenzy, and resolved on tearing down the theatre. And now was the crisis when Captain Rynders stepped forth and contradicted the report, told them the truth, and in short tickled the mob that they actually bore him off in their arms in triumph. The next adventure of the Captain was with O'Rourke himself, on board the cabin of a steamboat. O'Rourke had lost money to a gentleman at faro, got angry, and attempted to take his life. At that time Captain Rynders knew nothing of the game, but was assured by others that O'Rourke was in the wrong, and that his money had been fairly won. This was enough for Captain Rynders. He seized a red-hot poker, and actually drove the pugilist out of the cabin. O’Rourke afterwards acknowledged his error and became the fast friend of Rynders. Severely afflicted with sickness at New Orleans, and unsuccessful in obtaining business, in about six months after his arrival there, Captain Rynders again returned to New York, for the holy purpose, which for twenty years he has steadily fulfilled, of taking care of his aged parents. Again returning to New Orleans, his life was little else than a series of personal encounters and adventures, mainly on other persons' account. On one occasion at a masquerade ball, a fight arose between a couple of Virginians and several Frenchmen, with whom the majority present appeared to take part. Obeying the impulses of his nature, Captain Rynders took up for the Virginians, who seemed ready and willing to fight, and at it they went. Bowie knives were drawn, and used; pistols were fired, and the fight became furious. In the melee Captain Rynders received several severe cuts upon the back of his neck and elsewhere, the marks of which he will carry to his grave. A pistol was fired at his head, the ball passing through his hat, and slightly grazing the left side of his head. We next find our Captain in the Calaboose, for whipping a couple of gens d’armes, who had attacked an old man at the theatre. Not then understanding their true character as policemen, Captain Rynders mistook them for common soldiers, who had no rights above common citizens. In this fight, after receiving more wounds and scars, he whipped the gens d’armes, who went away, and returned with the whole guard of twelve. To this guard, as he understood their character, Captain Rynders surrendered with the honors of war. As soon as explanation was made for the charge, Captain Rynders was let go. At New Orleans, his pockets were always open to strangers in necessity, from the North. Many can attest to his liberality, while few can remember that they have ever repaid it. One gentleman will certainly remember that he forgot to hand over to Captain Rynders' mother several hundred dollars, which he had despatched by him to her. At Natchez, Capt. Rynders figured extensively and always as a leader of every circle in which he chanced to be, whether in bar room or ballroom, at the theatre or the course, at meetings religious or political. On one occasion a young man, a stranger to him, was, for some cause, believed to be unjustifiable, seized by the mob, who had resolved on summarily lynching him. Capt. Rynders promptly and enthusiastically resolved that they should do no such thing. He immediately raised a small party of fifteen or twenty friends, rushed in among the lynchers, and with bowie knife in one hand and pistol in the other, rescued the young man from his frightful situation, and bore him off to safety. Upon the Mississippi Captain Rynders was well known, and became almost as famous for his exploits as Paul Jones in the Northern Seas. His adventurous and hair-breadth escapes would fill a volume. In female intercourse, and in all matters of love, Captain Rynders has always eminently distinguished himself, and thought, felt, said, done his share. But other matters of this kind now engross the public attention, we shall pass them over with brief allusion to an affair of honor, in which a fair Helen was concerned, which occurred on his passage, upon a certain occasion, up to Wheeling. A gentleman had insulted the wife of one of the passengers on board. Such circumstance could not transpire either without the knowledge of Captain Rynders, or without his taking up the quarrel. He did take it up in defense of the lady. Challenge to mortal combat was the consequence. The Captain was known to be a Yankee, and his opponent was no little surprised at his prompt acceptance of his challenge. He chose pistols--seconds were selected--the case became serious to the principals while outsiders anticipated rich sport and bets ran high that the Yankee would get shot. At the instance of all the passengers the boat was stopped, and the parties went ashore to fight.

The latter called upon two negro women, who were at work in the same field, for assistance but instead of helping they fell upon him with their hoes and soon put him to death. The three negroes secreted the body of Mr. Boyd in a brush heap but in two days time it began to smell, they removed it to a log pile, set everything on fire, and burnt the body to ashes. spellchecked: Negro, a fiend, truly, who deserved the utmost severity of the offended laws, was hurried from the county jail of this county, and burnt at the stake - and not even a bill of indictment was found by our grand jury against the well-known participants in the act. Recently, a respited criminal was taken from the jail of a neighboring county, and executed by the populace - and we have heard of legal proceedings against the leaders of the mob. In the counties bordering on the western frontier, the lynching process, for years has competed with the civil, almost to the exclusion of the latter - a fact notorious in those regions, and which the writer is prepared to prove. Last winter, a stranger was shot in Buchanan County, in endeavoring to escape from flogging, the penalty of a suspicion of being connected with counterfeiters and no investigation made of the matter. In Independence, recently, it was declared by two of the most influential citizens of that place, that had they been present when certain of the participants in the Chavis affair were arrested, those persons should have been immediately executed - the writer has reason to believe it was no empty declaration. As it was, they were maltreated by the mob; men too, who have since been proven to have had little to do with that transaction - while others were coerced to make statements, under pain of death, which ultimately may convict the innocent. These are facts which can be sustained by irrefragable testimony - and it is but justice when we are considering the causes which lead to the aspersions of constitutional writers, that we should consider them and utter against them our condemnation. To pass them silently over, were to admit the validity of what is not true - that they are the offspring of a form of government which is the interest of the anti-republican to vilify. Though lynch law is so common in this country, it is by no means peculiar to it, a fact which our calumniators seem entirely to overlook. In fact, there is reason to believe that the very term is of European origin. In a late work on Ireland (Thackeray's Irish Sketch Book, p. 70) we are informed, in substance, that 'there is in Deadman's Lane, Galway, "raw head and bones over door," commemorative of the following tragic affair. In 1493, the Mayor of Galway, James Fitzstephen Lynch, came to the knowledge of a murder committed by his son, some years before at sea. Hereon, the culprit, was arraigned before his own father, and sentenced to death. The clan Lynch, however, rose in body to rescue the young man, and avert such a disgrace from their family, but the father, another Lucius Junius Brutus, frustrated their designs by hanging his son with his own hands!' If this case did not give origin to the phrase; it certainly deserved the application. Alison himself admits and laments the frequent occurrence of popular outbreaks in Europe - that even the hero of Waterloo himself was 'reviled by majority of his countrymen, execrated by the mob, narrowly escaping death from their hands.' Yet, the existence of misrule in Europe cannot apologize for its existence here. Recrimination can effect but little of good in any case, as 'two wrongs can never make a right.' Let then, being satisfied of the necessity of the supremacy of law, to our ultimate well-being as a nation, use every exertion to maintain that supremacy, and abide the issue.

Recently , a respited criminal was taken from the jail of a neighboring county , and executed by the populace - and we have heard of legal proceedings against the leaders of the mob . In the counties bordering on the western frontier , the lynching process , for years has competed with the civil , almost to the exclusion of the latter - a fact notorious in those regions , and which the writer is prepared to prove . Last winter , a stranger was shot in Buchanan County , in endeavoring to escape from flogging , the penalty of a suspicion of being connected with counterfeiters and no investigation made of the matter . In Independence , recently , it was declared by two of the most influential citizens of that place , that had they been present when certain of the participants in the Chavis affair were arrested , those persons should have been immediately executed - the writer has reason to believe it was no empty declaration . As it was , they were maltreated by the mob ; men too , who have since been proven to have had little to do with that transaction - while others were coerced to make statements , under pain of death , which ultimately may convict the innocent . These are facts which can be sustained by irrefragable testimony - and it is but justice when we are considering the causes which lead to the aspersions of constitutional writers , that we should consider them and utter against them our condemnation . To pass them silently over , were to admit the validity of what is not true - that they are the offspring of a form of government which is the interest of the anti-republican to vilify . Though lynch law is so common in this country , it is by no means peculiar to it , a fact which our calumniators seem entirely to overlook . In fact , there is reason to believe that the very term is of European origin

The Negro Outrage. In the last number of our paper, we gave an imperfect account of the summary punishment of five Negro robbers belonging to Mr. Burnly, of this county hung according to statute of law such cases made and provided. We learned the particulars of the crime that led to their execution and the more we reflect on them, the more we incline to approve any step calculated to punish the, for such revolting outrage as they acknowledged was by them committed. It appears that they went to the house during his absence, and ordered his wife to give them some liquor. On her refusing, they cursed her in blasphemous terms and threatened her with violence if she did not comply. After having gotten the liquor, they demanded hot coffee and cold victuals, which they said she would have to provide if she would not have her children harmed, which they promised to do. After this, they forcibly took from her an infant babe and rudely threw it upon the floor, they threw her down, and while one accomplished the fiendish designs of a rape, the other pointed the muzzle of a loaded gun at her head and said he would blow out her brains if she resisted or made the least noise. They afterwards took the quilts and blankets from the bed, broke open the trunks and drawers, and rifled their contents, which consisted of forty dollars in specie and a quantity of clothing, all of which they carefully put up in the quilts and blankets. They even took the shoes from off the feet of the woman and placing the whole of the plunder on the back of a horse which they had brought with them for the purpose, they made off. We obtained these particulars from a gentleman of the highest responsibility. He questioned the negroes on the subject a few hours prior to their execution and also interrogated Mrs. Burnly in a similar manner, and her answers agreed in every essential particular with the statements made by the negroes. What aggravates this affair is the fact that the unfortunate woman had but six weeks previously recovered from childbirth and her body is bruised and much hurt from the rough treatment she received while in the hands of the negroes, the prints of whose fingers were visible on her neck. We have ever been, and now are, opposed to any kind of punishment being administered under the statutes of Judge Lynch, but when we reflect upon what must be the feelings of the husband and father, and the deep anguish which must invade the bosom of the injured wife and outraged mother, due regard for candor and the preservation of all that is held most sacred and all that is most dear to man in the domestic circle of life, impels us to acknowledge the fact that if the perpetrators of this excessively revolting crime had been burnt alive, as was first decreed, their fate would have been too good for such diabolical and inhuman wretches.-Gallatin Signal, 11th instant

The game, as a matter of course, was blocked at once, and demonstration immediately made that the gambler should fork over his ill-gotten gains. This he flatly refused to do; said that he had won the money fair, and that he was very clear of parting with what he had come honestly by. They still persisted, and he still refused. The boat then stopped to wood, when the men, finding it useless to attempt regaining their money by fair means, resorted to a plan which the gambler undoubtedly thought foul. We are authorized to give the following statement of facts to that affair by gentlemen present and an eyewitness of the transaction. Several of the Banks instituted suits in the Circuit Court of Yazoo county against the citizens discounted in Bank. Among them one in favor of the Benton and Manchester Railroad Bank against Dr. Riddell. The defendants plead usury. On the trial, there was no evidence to sustain other than that the Bank paid the proceeds of the discounted note, on which the suit was instituted, in its own notes during its suspension of specie payments, which had since changed. The jury, after deliberating for two days, returned a special verdict in favor of the plaintiff for the amount the note and interest, payable in the notes of the Benton and Manchester Railroad Bank, or their equivalent. The informed the jury that the verdict was not legal, nor was it in a form that would justify the court. They must find a specific verdict for the plaintiff or find generally for the defendant. He further instructed them that the fact of the notes of the Bank devalued at the time of the negotiation of the note was no evidence that the Bank had taken usurious interest. They returned to their room, and again appeared and informed the judge that they could not agree on any other verdict. The counsel for the Bank agreed to withdraw a juror, and make a mistrial, and agreed to continue all of the Bank roles in consequence of the excitement of the people against the Banks, which seemed to have reached the jurors, under the hope and expectation that the excitement would subside before the next term. The judge sanctioned the continuation of the cases and commented on the extraordinary and peculiar state of things that existed in the country. He remarked he had never before known a County jury to differ so widely on a question of law, which seemed to have been brought about by the members of the bar, some of whom were employed against the Banks. Although he had no doubt of the honest intentions and pure motives of the jurors, he remarked that such an extraordinary state of things was calculated to subvert the ends of justice. Some of the jury, as well as the members of the bar, misconstrued the remarks of the judge and presented him as having said that the conduct of the jurors was calculated to subvert the ends of justice. Much excitement was produced among the jurors and people in the court yard. A member of the bar informed the judge that the remarks had been misconstrued by the jurors. The judge called the jurors and explained what he did say. The jurors asked the judge whether he had not made use of the offensive mentioned attributed to him. The judge answered that he did not. Col. Alston, standing without the bar, replied: you did say so, the judge ordered him to be fined a hundred dollars for contempt of court. This explanation did not seem to satisfy the populace, who were already agitated on the Bank question, some under artificial stimulants, and they became more clamorous and noisy and collected in considerable numbers around and near the court-house threatening the judge in bitter terms and menacing him with personal violence. It was on Thursday evening. When court adjourned, the judge left out at the front door of the house on his way to his lodgings when he was pursued by Col. Alston, who requested an interview. Vicksburg has been the scene of another disorderly and illegal proceeding, which resulted in bloodshed and death. It seems that some ten or fifteen persons, ardent lovers of justice and social order, armed themselves with muskets, ropes, etc., and proceeded, about 1 o'clock on Thursday night the 23rd ult., to inflict summary justice upon a family of four Germans, named Flekenstein, (a father and three sons,) who lived in the upper part of the town, and who, it was said, kept a disorderly house. They demanded admission. This being refused, they broke open the outer door and entered, J. A. Helt, a German, and an unusually rash and adventurous young fop, leading the way. Before he entered he called to his comrades 'who will go in with me if I lead the way?' Several replied that they would. The family was in the upper story of the house. He commenced ascending the stairs, when, perhaps dreading the resistance of some one he saw, or more effectively to clear the way, he discharged one of his pistols and wounded one of the sons of Flekenstein severely in the neck and jaws. A volley of four or five shots was almost instantly returned. Helt fell dead, piece of the skull being torn off and almost the whole of the brains dashed out. His comrades seeing him fall, suddenly took to their heels and no more was seen of them. Some other names have been communicated to us, but we refrain from giving them at present, lest we should either injure innocent individuals or prejudice the administration of justice. It is thought that the wounds of Flekenstein will not seriously endanger his life. Infamous. - A few days ago, a sum of money was stolen near Kosciusko, Mississippi. A black girl, who professed to know all about the circumstances, charged a respectable white person with being the thief. Upon her testimony, the citizens seized him, tied him to a tree and 'lynched' him with extreme severity: looking on, men exclaiming - 'Give it to him! He has the money! He is the thief and will soon confess!' The lynchers found, however, after nearly killing their victim, that he would confess nothing and he was at length released, torn, bleeding, and unable to stand. Few hours afterwards, suspicion began to rest upon Parker himself who, on being tied to the tree, cried out 'I have the money!' The whole sum was found in his possession and that of the wench on whose false testimony the innocent man had been so horribly mutilated. This occurrence should be a memorable lesson to all who are disposed to take the vengeance of the law into their own hands. The Massacre of Seventy Missionaries The New Bedford Mercury of Saturday, contains a statement of the most horrid massacre of seventy native missionaries at Wallis Island in the South Sea, in August, 1835. Mr. William N.J. Barnard, formerly Second Officer on the ship Selma, of New Bedford, who arrived there in the Parachute a few days since, furnished the statement to the Mercury. It appears from his journal that the English Missionaries at Keppel Island, one of the Friendly group, conceived the extraordinary plan of attempting to introduce Christianity at Wallis Island, by sending native teachers and missionaries, thinking they would meet with less opposition than foreigners. They procured them passage to the island; horrid to relate, soon after they landed, the whole number were murdered in the most barbarous and inhumane manner. Mr. Barnard was at the island at the time the massacre took place, and left in the sloop of war Vincennes when she touched at that place. He left the latter vessel at Cape Town. It appears that in the vicinity of Auburn there is a knave by the name of Sweets who has gathered around him half a score of silly women, who believe him to possess extraordinary powers, and bound to obey him under all circumstances at all times. To prove their obedience to him was their duty, they are on one occasion ordered by him to take a carving knife, and proceed through the street and slay whatever might impede his progress. She entered upon her task and had it not been the instrument of death wrested from her hand by the first person she attacked, she would have obeyed his command to the letter. On another occasion, he commanded three of the women to proceed on a Sabbath day to a neighboring church where communion was about to be administered, to upset the table, scatter the vessels and drink up the wine. Accordingly, at the proper hour, they entered the house singing and dancing as they proceeded and performed the duty assigned them. These outrages incensed the neighborhood, and it was secretly determined by a few who had imbibed an attachment to the code of Judge Lynch, to present the whole household with a coat of tar and feathers. For this purpose, some ten or twelve young men blackened their faces and otherwise disguised themselves, and proceeded at a late hour on Monday or Tuesday night of last week, to Sweet's house, which they entered, seized several of the inmates, (among whom was Sweet) covered their bodies with tar, and then feathered them with the contents of a bed which they took from the house for that purpose. The intruders then retired but again soon returned and stole a large quantity of maple sugar, with which they decamped. On making their second visit, one of the disguised gentlemen was recognized and the next day arrested, examined, and bound over for trial. spellchecked: THE REIGN OF TERROR SOUTH. Letter from a Minnesotan in New Orleans—The Murder of the Three Carpenters at Friar's Point. True! The St. Anthony News of the 3rd published a letter from Alderman McHerron of that city, who was recently in New Orleans in relation to the treatment received by himself and another Minnesotan, and Northerners generally, in the South, and confirming the atrocious murder of the three carpenters at Friar's Point, Mississippi. The News says: The wife of Ald. McHerron, this city, received yesterday the following letter from her husband, who is now in Cincinnati. It adds another to the list of outrages with which the press is teeming. It is difficult to appreciate the intensity of mingled fear and hate and madness which pervade a community where such outrages are permitted. Mr. McHerron is a well-known citizen of St. Anthony. Mr. Coggs well was recently Deputy Sheriff for this county. There may be some in this community debased enough to betray these gentlemen to the peril of their lives, but we are happy not to know them! I will now give you a brief history of the causes that led me to come to this place, and will in the first place state briefly that it was to save my life. There is a reign of terror in New Orleans, as well as in the whole South. A Northern man holds his life in his hands after getting below Memphis, but nothing to what it is below there. After getting as far as Vicksburg, a Northern man is abused on the smallest pretense imaginable, and if there is a gin house or other building burnt, from any cause whatever, the cry is raised that it is the work of an abolitionist, and woe to the Northern man that is found in the neighborhood. If he escapes being hung, he will be shaved on the head, and branded on his cheek or forehead. If the punishment is meant to be light, he may be tarred and feathered, rode on a rail, and then started to the nearest place to a steamboat or the cars, being abused all the way and started North on deck passage, and if he has no money, to depend on the charity of those he may happen to be with to keep from starving. This is no overdrawn picture, but it does not picture half the enormities practiced by the chivalry of the South. There have been scores of men lynched and hung in the South from no other cause than being Northern Republicans. Although other charges, such as exciting slaves, and giving them poison and arms and ammunition to kill their masters with, are trumped up against them. The matter of hanging three men at Friar's Point, you have no doubt seen in the papers, also a denial of it afterwards by the Southern press, as also that the letter purporting to be written by Halle giving the account of it was a forgery. But I tell you that it is verily believed, a fact, that those three men were hung as stated, but they wish to cover that like the others. You don't hear of one case in fifty that is perpetrated. The policy of the press in the South is to suppress the publication of these things, and when they are published it is the exception rather than the rule. It is a truly horrible state of affairs. In New Orleans there is not even an allusion made to what has been done there, and yet I can furnish proof, if any statement is doubted, that there were, the week before I left, six men hung for being abolitionists, as all Republicans are called, in the city of New Orleans. There have been scores without limit driven from the city by the vigilance committee, so styled. I am, or rather, was informed while in New Orleans that the course taken by those guardians of Southern rights and Southern honor is to ascertain former residence and then write to the subservient tools of the South in the North to find out what the man's politics have been, and if he has been honest enough to act a Republican, he gets his notice to leave instanter. The usual limit is twenty-four hours, and it was on a request of that kind that I left—choosing to leave rather than run the risk of being taken out the next night and hung to a lamp post. You may think such things strange, but nevertheless they are true. I could not write to you to warn you not to write me anything politically that would compromise me, fearing that the letter would be opened and read, thereby precipitating the very thing I was anxious to avoid. But I am thankful that your own good sense guided you in the matter and that you avoided all things of the kind. There were several of my letters opened; some of them were resealed and some had written on the envelope "opened by mistake by another person." Amongst that number, the one you wrote me immediately after election, but you had the information so worded, calling them Black Republicans, that there could be no advantage taken. Mr. G. Coggs well was also driven away. He was notified at eleven o'clock on Saturday night to leave on Sunday. He could not arrange his business by the time the train went out on Sunday evening, and was positively hid until 1 o'clock next morning and then left. He had been to St. Louis, and only got back to New Orleans on the evening he was notified to leave. Doesn't it seem hard that such things should exist in this country? Yet such is the case. I would have remained in New Orleans this winter had I not been interfered with. But it would have been foolhardy in me to have resisted or not complied with their "very moderate request." S.S.F. Time does take the buckram out of all the saintly gentry, etc.

spellchecked: SUICIDE OF LYNCHER IN IOWA.—In Cedar county, Iowa, a young man named Finch, son of a church deacon, and member of a vigilance committee, led away by evil companions and the counsels of men who should have set a better example, was present when the life or death of two horse thieves, one named Kelso, was hanging in the balance. The lynchers took a vote on the subject, and when the fatal hat came round, Finch dropped into it his ballot, inscribed with the word "Death." On counting the ballots, a majority were found to have declared that the culprits should die, and Kelso and his comrade were accordingly hung to a neighboring tree. Young Finch, after witnessing their dying struggles, went home, when his mother anxiously asked him if the thieves had been caught. "Yes," he told her, "and hung, and he had voted to hang them." His mother sadly and solemnly told him he had no right unlawfully to take that which he could not give—the life of a fellow being—and continued a few moments speaking of the enormity of the act. He then left her and went out to plough, but after ploughing a few furrows, he tied his horse, took off one of the reins, and with it hung himself to the lower limb of a tree. When found, his knees almost touched the ground, and he evidently could have arisen to his feet at pleasure had he changed his purpose before insensibility supervened. All attempts to restore the unhappy youth to life proved useless. The affair produced considerable feeling among the members of the vigilance committee.

The town was growing sensibly duller. Many were leaving, and Indian troubles deterred people from coming in. Provisions high and scarce. A vigilance committee was about organizing to lynch a butcher, but it was promptly nipped in the bud. In reference to the war the Colonel says, unless help in the way of provisions, etc., is furnished by California, the volunteers must disband and the whole fighting given up to two hundred regulars on foot, in which event he fears depopulation of the Territory, as the signs of a long and bloody war are imminent. Unless the American troops can meet the savages in a few days and give them a severe lesson in a great battle, the worst is anticipated. When leaving Virginia City, Col. Hays told his troops that unless they were willing to live on meat for some time, the road was open to Carson City and they were at liberty to take it. Not a man left. A great battle was expected to come off on Sunday last. The Colonel says Nevada and Sierra came nobly to the relief of their brethren in Utah; Sacramento did something, but not more than enough to pay for stolen horses. San Francisco, with millions at stake, had done nothing. Correspondence of the Herald. WILKES-BARRE, Pa., 9th August, 1856. Messrs. Editors: My prediction in a previous letter to the Herald, concerning Gov. Reeder's removal, has been verified; and the people of Kansas must now experience the relief, felt by a sleeper under an incubus, when suddenly restored to wakefulness. The explanations demanded by the President of his Excellency, touching the charges of illegal land speculations, came forth as clear as a black cloud in a dark night; and have had the effect to disappoint his friends throughout the country egregiously. His defense embraces but two material points. The first, in regard to the purchase of Indian lands, he answers in the following language:—"If there is any wrong in the matter, it is not "a wrong committed," but at most only a wrong "attempted," and in the face of all probability a wrong which we expected to be sanctioned by the President." The second point is simply a demurrer! i.e., the Governor does not deny his guilt in "other speculations in the lands of Kansas, apparently in violation of Acts of Congress, &c.," but that "the very general manner in which the charges are stated, the entire absence of any specification on which to make a point or raise an issue" might cause him to "wander in side issues, departures, evasions and uncertainties, without ever reaching a conclusion." Pettifogging is generally contemplated, which even a bad case will not justify, but this position of the Governor is laughable. spellchecked: On Monday, the 1st inst., a short time before sunset, a man was found hanging upon a tree on the premises where the unfortunate Rochebave and Connout, the two cattle thieves, who were lynched last autumn, carried on their nefarious business. Upon investigation it appeared that on Sunday evening, July 1st, about 10 o'clock, a band of men, some 25 in number, came into San Antonio on horseback, entered the public house known as the "Antonio House," and forcibly dragged one John Fanning therefrom. The people of the village were generally asleep, no noise or tumult was created, and nothing was said or heard of John Fanning until he was discovered last evening hanging upon a tree as above stated. The deceased has for a long time been marked as a dissolute character, suspected of horse stealing, etc. It is evident that those who hung him were not actuated by any desire of gain, for even his pockets appeared unexamined, $25 being found upon his person when he was cut down. Up to this time no knowledge has been obtained of the parties concerned in the commission of the disgraceful outrage, or any of the particulars of the proceedings of the murdering band after they left the Antonio House with their victim. It is said that the deceased was very active in the hanging of Rochebave and Connout last autumn. What a comment on "mob law!" LATER.—Since writing the above we are informed the mob hung the wrong man, a person evidently innocent of the supposed crime. We clip the above from the Evening Journal of yesterday. spellchecked: The soil of Kentucky is red with the blood of men who died in fair combat, and those who have been butchered in cold blood. But of the latter, we know of no case more atrocious than the assassination of Thomas S. Lowe in the Hawesville Jail, yesterday, by a bloodthirsty and cowardly mob. A feud had existed for years between Lowe and Creeor Maxwell, Commonwealth's Attorney of that Judicial District, which had its origin in party politics. Lowe sent his adversary a challenge sometime since, which he refused to notice. Lowe then sent him word he would cowhide him on sight. Maxwell did not attend court at last term, and it is said for the reason he wished to avoid personal conflict with his determined and desperate foe. The Court met on Tuesday, and Lowe publicly declared Maxwell a poltroon and coward. The information was given to Maxwell, who armed himself and with a body of friends, attacked Lowe. The latter, as we related yesterday, retreated. A number of shots were fired, one of which killed a man named Aldridge or Eskring. Lowe was thought for a while the mob would lynch him, but finally he was taken to prison and disarmed. The town was feverish with excitement, and on Wednesday night, the mob, who of course hated Lowe (mobs always hate brave men), increased in numbers and the thirst for blood. During the night it was decided to force the Jail and lynch Lowe, or if they couldn't approach him, kill him outright. On yesterday morning, in accordance with the plans, the mob attacked the Jail, and fearing to lay hands upon their victim, fired upon him. He received some sixteen or eighteen balls in vital parts, and died. Glutted with vengeance, the mob then retired. Lowe leaves a family who reside in Hawesville. His father lives in this city. He was a cool, determined, and most dangerous man. In all of his brawls or shooting affairs, from which until this, he came out unscathed, he displayed an extraordinary degree of courage, and he doubtless died as he lived, without fear of mortal man. —Louisville Courier.

spellchecked: There was a way. The Express treated with great contempt, the other day, the complaints of several prominent and influential presses against Gov. Weller for not suppressing mob violence, and declared, as well as we recollect, that, according to "law and political science" in which it seemed to intimate that it was amazingly well posted, all that the Governor could do in cases of infractions of the law by mobs, was to wait until somebody resisted a civil process, which process it was the duty of subordinate officers to originate and enforce. It now concludes that there is a way in which the Governor can act ab initio in the premises, and says: "WE direct the attention of the newly converted "law and order" press, that are so distressed at the alarming prevalence of "mobocracy," and Gov. Weller's failure to enforce the law, to the fact that that functionary has issued a proclamation that may be more touching to their nervous systems than the late mob hangings were. Here follows the proclamation: WHEREAS, I have received satisfactory evidence that a band of lawless individuals did, on the 30th of Nov., 1858, at Los Angeles, force the County Jail and take therefrom a prisoner, one Pancho Daniel, and execute him without authority of law; and whereas, similar atrocious acts have been perpetrated in Tuolumne, and some of the other counties of this State, Now, therefore, by virtue of the authority in me vested by the constitution and laws of this State, I hereby offer a reward of ONE THOUSAND DOLLARS for the arrest and conviction of any, or either, of the persons or parties who have been engaged in these unlawful executions." Of course, this proclamation will simply amount to nothing, because, in order to enforce the law, it is necessary that public opinion should sustain it. In the eye of the law, every man engaged in those hanging operations is guilty of murder, but the people will not so consider it, and would refuse to allow one of their number to be interfered with on account of his connection with the transactions alluded to. Should the local judicial tribunals issue warrants for the arrest of the offending parties, and the ministerial officers undertake to execute them, the people would make resistance and protect each other to the bitter end. The officers would summon assistance from the body of the county, but it would not be forthcoming, for respectable citizens do not like to shoot down their equally respectable neighbors. Then, the Governor, being called upon, would order out "the volunteer or uniform companies or other militia of the State," but they would probably refuse, to any considerable extent, to respond to the call. If they did respond, then there would be civil war. Such is, we think, a well-founded view of the case, based on the present state of public opinion in California. It is a deplorable state of opinion, we will admit, and ought to be rectified. But, such being the condition of unpopular feeling, it is very doubtful whether Governor Weller has the nerve, despite his "boasted disregard of popular clamor," to press to an extremity the high-sounding declaration of his inaugural manifesto, to the effect that he would "maintain the supremacy of the law at all hazards." It is his sworn duty nevertheless to do this very thing, irrespective of any declarations that he may have made pro or con. It is certainly high time that lynch law were done away with in this country, and much do we fear that it will not cease for many years, unless some terrible example is made. But who will take the responsibility of that example?

A MAN HUNG BY A MOB.—A few weeks ago a constable named Simmons was shot by a man named Kessler, in Gentry County, [Mo.,] under circumstances which made the act, in the estimation of the people, a cruel outrage. The murderer was arrested and put in jail at Albany, and word sent to Judge Norton, at Platte City, that if a special term was not held immediately for the trial of the prisoner, he would be tried before Judge Lynch. Judge Norton called the special term as requested; but, on the trial, it was found that two of the prisoner's important witnesses had been driven off and could not be found. The counsel for the defense asked a continuance which was granted; and the Judge, inferring from the appearance of things that an attempt would be made by the crowd to take the prisoner out of the hands of the officers, appointed a guard of twenty-five men to conduct him to jail. But the guard had no sooner taken its position than a rush was made by the crowd, and the prisoner torn from the officers and borne off to the woods a few hundred yards distant. Arrived there, the prisoner was allowed to say his prayers, after which a rope was put around his neck and he was hung to a tree. The mob was composed of about fifty persons.—St. Louis News. He requested to be baptized, which was done in a brook nearby. Here he had an interview with his old father which was deeply affecting. He was then taken back to the tree and hung until dead." A MICROSCOPIC WONDER.—We have had the pleasure of seeing recently a microscopic photograph, which is a truly very remarkable curiosity. Upon the object glass appears a small speck, occupying the space of six by seven and a half hundredths of an inch—about the size of the square lead in an ordinary lead pencil before it is cut—appearing to the unaided vision only as a stain or slight discoloration upon the glass. But the microscope reveals it to be a complete copy of the Declaration of Independence, with the names of the signers in full, containing no less than 1,850 letters, each of which is a finished specimen of typography, and the whole, under a high magnifying power, can be seen with the utmost distinctness and read with the utmost ease. The letters are only one twenty-four hundredth of an inch in size, but are perfectly formed and elegant. This wonderful achievement of the photographic art was brought from Paris by Mr. D. P. Ives, and is the property of Dr. George A. Perkins, Salem Register.

spellchecked: The arrival of the Prometheus brings us fifteen days later intelligence from California, by way of the newly-opened route of San Juan de Nicaragua. The prominent, and by far the most conspicuous feature of the California news is the prevalence of what would be called on this side of the continent the supreme authority of Judge Lynch. In San Francisco, it is the execution of the decrees of the Vigilance Committee of Five Hundred (not quite so ceremonious as the old Venetian Council), in the prompt punishment of criminals, and for the preservation of law and order. Strange as it may sound in this longitude, these off-hand trials and summary executions are, in good faith, designed for the preservation, rather than the restoration, of law and order. The criminal may be a murderer, a horse thief, burglar, an incendiary, a common shoplifter, or petty rogue; if the Vigilance Committee catch him and convict him, he is instantly carried out and hung up at the nearest convenient tree, or beam, or rope and tackle. The crime, the pursuit, the apprehension, the indictment, the trial, the judgment, and the execution, may all take place in the same afternoon. The whole business, in the case of Jenkins, was done in the course of an evening, by moonlight; and in the case of Stuart, another Botany convict, tried also as a thief, the interval between the commencement of his trial and the hanging was about five hours. In the case of the Mexican woman at Downieville—who, for fatally stabbing a miner, was tried by the popular process in such cases established, and convicted of murder—the blood of her victim was not yet cold, when the woman, having been tried, convicted, and condemned, was swinging lifeless in the air. The Anglo-Saxon institution of the rope, by a sort of 'charter of popular justice,' or 'course of summary judgment,' may be considered as pretty well established in California; but the rapidity with which it brings the criminal to his quietus is somewhat startling to a community accustomed to the slower formalities of law. This quickness of the penalty is even more astounding to our preconceived notions than the rapidity of crimes which come under the death penalty by the new California code. We have no nice distinction between murder and manslaughter, nor between highway robbery and a petty theft: the same judgment of strangulation makes short work of them all. Truly, this is a terrible state of things and is deeply to be deplored. But the people of California, it appears, not only have reasonable excuses for these summary and indiscriminate executions, but their situation is such as imperatively to demand them. The Australian convicts of England, the most desperate and lawless vagabonds from every nation under the sun, have been concentrating their forces in California since the golden discovery—

spellchecked: on Wednesday morning from San Juan de Nicaragua, bringing California dates to the 10th of July. The Prometheus has brought on freight $57,579 in gold dust, besides what she may have brought in the hands of passengers, who number three hundred and sixty. She left San Juan on Monday, August 4, at 11 A.M., and arrived at Staten Island, below New York, on the 18th instant, at 11 o'clock P.M., making the passage in eight days and twelve hours, bringing her passengers from the steamer Pacific, which left San Francisco on the 14th ultimo, and arrived at San Juan del Sud on the 29th, with four hundred and twenty-five passengers and $500,000 in gold dust. We learn from the New York Tribune that the passengers by the Nicaragua route came fifteen miles by land carriage; thence took the steamer Director across Lake Nicaragua; thence the new iron steamer Sir Henry L. spellchecked: THE EXECUTION OF JENKINS.—The sudden, unusual, and solemn occurrence which transpired during the night of the 10th instant and the succeeding morning produced throughout our city yesterday a feverish state of excitement. The assumption of authority by a body of respectable citizens, the enforcement of a sentence of death upon a condemned murderer in the dead hour of night, without the usual forms of law, may well create an unusual stir in any community. Deprived of the benefit of laws, and powerless to compel their enforcement, our citizens have been at the mercy of organized gangs of the worst villains that infested our city and preyed upon its inhabitants. Our citizens have been robbed and murdered, our fair city destroyed by the torch of the incendiary, and hundreds of honest young men stripped of their hard-earned gains and their prospects in life ruined. Such a state of affairs could no longer be borne. Against every principle of self-preservation and forbearance, patience and mercy had absolutely ceased. The time had arrived when the people were compelled for the safety of their lives and the protection of their property to take the law into their own hands, and inflict terrible punishment upon the guilty. Extraordinary circumstances justify extraordinary measures and the administration of punishment. The first act in the drama has been enacted, and the felon has paid with his life the penalty of his crimes. We have never been advocates of mob lynch law, snatching from the hands of legal tribunals the powers legitimately conferred upon them, of depriving any of the benefit of a fair and impartial trial by his fellow-men. Yet, in the present condition of municipal affairs, we cannot conscientiously condemn the people for the course they have felt themselves compelled to adopt. Deeply deploring the occasion for the exercise of such acts, we admit that necessity absolutely demanded the assumption of power. The trial and conviction of Jenkins was not the act of an inflamed and excited mob. His case was adjudged with calmness and deliberation, his guilt fully established, and the penalty of death imposed by a body of men respected and esteemed by their fellows, assuming the responsibility imposed upon them by necessity, with a full perception of their accountability to their fellow-men and their Maker. Who but He shall adjudge and condemn them? We dare not. There may be difference of opinion—there is, undoubtedly, as to the punishment of burglary and petty larceny.
