But while all this is going on, alarming enough in principle, but, wonderful to say, creating no alarm in practice, the tribunals in all civil matters are recognized and obeyed, just as they are in more established and in older States. Nay, even nice distinctions are drawn between the apparently conflicting jurisdictions of Lynch law and the statute law, or law of the land; for we see in the St. Marysville (Cal.) Herald before us that the vigilance committee of that place declined to interfere in a Mexican brawl where knives had been used, and murder almost perpetrated, upon the ground that the case was not one for them, but for the statute law. The illustration is so singular and significant that we must give our readers the case in full. A Mexican, it seems, attacked by three other Mexicans at St. Marysville, and was so severely wounded by knife cuts that he was not expected to survive. He received seven or eight severe wounds. The cause of the attack is said to have been a dispute, which arose a few evenings since at a Mexican fandango, says the St. Marysville Herald. The vigilance committee very promptly arrested two of the men; the other one had not been taken. The committee examined the two men; the evidence appeared very conclusive; but, upon a cool and dispassionate review of the whole case, they determined "not to inflict punishment upon them, not deeming it a case in which they were warranted to proceed. They therefore handed them over to the authorities." But, adds the editor: "Justice Ellet examined the men, and detained them till it can be ascertained if the wounds inflicted upon their unfortunate victim shall prove mortal. If so, the charge against the men will be found to have been with intent to kill. In either event, the trial must be prompt.—"MUST," in italics, significant of Lynch law. 'We think the citizens will commend the action of the vigilance committee. The purpose of that committee is not to punish offenders of this class, but those who commit wanton attacks upon the peace and property of the community; such crimes as are more extended in their consequences, and the extent of which cannot be known when they are committed. It is no part of the committee's business to take cognizance of private quarrels, however fatal their consequences, except it be found that those whom the law makes the guardian of the citizen are lax or negligent of their duty. But let not the proper tribunal delay this case; the trial must be prompt, and the punishment must speedily follow conviction, if the parties be convicted; otherwise the vigilance committee will yet take the matter into their own hands. The trial must be prompt and the punishment must speedily follow conviction.' The editor speaks by the authority of Lynch; but in the distinctions here drawn between the jurisdiction of the court of Lynch and the courts of law, we see the difference yet paid to the civil and statute law. What is remarkable, nay, astonishing, is that Lynch law is becoming the popular law of the land. The San Francisco Herald, disproving the rumor that the Governor is about to convoke an extraordinary session of the Legislature in order to reinvigorate the laws of the land, exclaims: "The truth is, we are getting on remarkably well! This city is more free from crime than it ever has been within recollection, and the measures being taken by the vigilance committee will make it still more so. We are fast and imperceptibly getting rid of all the vagabonds who have been plundering and murdering so long with impunity. It is true, we have still a wretched judiciary; we have a very inefficient police, but the citizens are about to correct all that by degrees. They have set a mark on the forehead of the Judge, and they have assumed the duty of the police. There is a conviction in the minds of all that punishment will now closely follow the heels of crime, and that crime can scarcely be committed without detection. It is true that yet there are many things wanting, but what we do not want is an extra session of the last Legislature. We have many difficulties to contend with, but really that would be burdening us beyond our strength and patience. "A great deal is said about the prevalence of Lynch law throughout the country. Some three or four hundred warlike Indians have put to death twelve horse thieves. Well, there is nothing very deplorable in that. We are glad to know that there is a force of a sort to restrain such depredations in the lower country; and while the native Californians have such force, we hope they will always call it into requisition against such villains. Four men have been hung for murder, and two persons shot in a melee at the place. It is, to be sure, to be regretted that the murder was committed, and that the melee was provoked; but nevertheless the death of those four persons was perfectly natural consequences, the necessity of which was to be deplored of course, but nevertheless natural and unavoidable. In this city a man has been executed for burglary—a man belonging to a gang of robbers, assassins, and incendiaries. Lynch law, no doubt—but just law—punishment rendered necessary by the prevalence of crime. In all these cases we find no injustice, and in those in which the citizens are the avengers of the violated law, no haste, passion, or thirst for blood. A firm determination there is to mete out punishment where it is deserved, and that determination will be persevered in, whether there be an extra session of the Legislature at Vallejo or not." This is cool, complacent even. The attachment of the people to the law is apparent from their quiet submission to it. The committees of vigilance proceed, we see, with great system in all parts. At St. Marysville, there was a meeting of the committees held at the courthouse. The organization of the committee was completed. There were five hundred and thirteen signers. It is the intention of the committee to take a complete census of the city, keeping a record of the name and occupation of every one. Locations in which there is any hesitancy in giving this information, or where the manner of doing so is at all suspicious, will be strictly watched, says the narrator of the scene. In all parts of California, like proceedings are going on. This apparently necessary subversion of the civil and statute law is more or less than a revolution, bloodless though it be; but what must astonish mankind is the quietude in which it is all done. The American element of self-government is purging itself of the dangerous foreign admixtures that have got into the State. We have one other lesson in this spectacle, and that is, the danger of opening a State, as California has been opened, to the convicts and criminals of the whole earth. Botany Bay, and all the other British penal settlements in the Pacific, have vomited their criminals upon this rising State. The criminals of Chile, of Peru, of all Mexico, have fled there for an asylum. Our States this side of the Rocky Mountains have no doubt disgorged their share of murderers, thieves, robbers, burglars, &c.—criminals whom our police and our laws could overawe here, but who run riot in California. Such facts as these the Californians offer as their apology for the subversion of the statute law, and the establishment of Lynch law in its stead. spellchecked: ARRIVAL OF THE EMPIRE CITY. Late from California. Destructive Conflagration—City Hall and City Hospital in Ruins—Mining Intelligence—Horrible Murders—Assassins Lynched by the People—The Markets, &c., &c. NEW YORK, August 6—10 A.M.—The Empire City has arrived, having left Chagres on the 25th, and Kingston on the 30th of July. She brings three hundred and sixty passengers, and $400,900 freight; passengers also bring $500,600. Her mails bring San Francisco dates to July first. She left the Georgia at Chagres, awaiting the arrival of the Isthmus and Union at Panama. The Empire City encountered strong easterly gales during her passage. June 22d. It commenced on the north side of Pacific Street, near Powell, at ten o'clock in the morning, spreading down Pacific Street, through Broadway and on to Stockton Street. In half an hour it crossed Pacific Street, and at the same time crossed Stanton Street, spreading rapidly down Pacific, Broadway, and Jackson Streets. All in Broadway, as far as Jackson Street, was destroyed. On Pacific Street it extended as far as Ohio Street, taking the City Hall and City Hospital in its course. On Jackson Street everything was burned to Montgomery Street, including a few houses below on Stockton Street. The fire then crossed diagonally into Washington Street, in the rear of the Baptist church, which was saved. It thence extended down Washington and Dupont Streets, taking the Jackson House in its course. The California restaurant, adjoining the Alta California office, was blown up, but did not prevent the flames from crossing in the rear of the Verandah and extending down Washington Street to Sansome, stopping on the south side at Burgoyne's building. On Montgomery Street, the west side is burnt from Pacific to Washington Street, and also all the east side, with the exception of two or three buildings near the corner of Jackson Street. Between Washington and Clay Streets the only building burned was occupied by Cronan & Markley. From Washington Street the fire crossed over in the rear of the El Dorado to the new theater, which was destroyed. The flames then spread to Merchant Street, and thence crossed into Clay Street, below the California Exchange, on the north side. Thence the fire extended to the brick building occupied by Rolland & Wilde, at the corner of Montgomery Street. Immense quantities of goods were removed to the Plaza, which took fire and were destroyed. The patients in the hospital, numbering ninety, all saved and removed to a lot in the rear of the hospital. The prisoners in the city prison were removed to the county jail, and all the books and records in the marshal's office were saved. The buildings on the Plaza not burnt are the custom house, the Bella Union, Verandah, El Dorado, and Union Hotels, and the California Exchange. The wooden buildings between the latter and the Union Hotel were also saved. The Presbyterian Church on Stockton Street was burned. Chas. S. Lyons was burnt, and also Mr. Bach, of the firm of Bach, Burnet, & Co. In all, about five hundred buildings were destroyed, and the loss is estimated at $3,000,000. Immense quantities of lumber were consumed. The persons burnt out are generally insured. The fire was undoubtedly the work of incendiaries, and several persons have been arrested, but positive proof of their guilt has not been adduced. Few heavy stocks of goods were burnt, most of the buildings being occupied as dwellings. The excitement created since the fire against the desperadoes living amongst us has resulted in the determination on the part of the citizens to prevent the landing of persons from penal colonies, unless they produce testimonials of character. The proceedings of the vigilance committee have been generally sustained by the community. Captain Snow, a worthy citizen of Sonora, has been murdered by two assassins, and in two days afterwards the ruffians were taken and hung by the populace, under the most intense excitement. In Carson's diggings two Americans and some four or five Mexicans were killed. A large number of Mormons from Salt Lake Valley had arrived at Los Angeles. Colonel Barbour, of the Indian commission, has been compelled to suspend operations for want of funds. Dr. Wozencraft was progressing at his own expense. Two men, named Watkins and Briar, had been convicted of burglary and sentenced—one to ten and the other to five years imprisonment. A party of nine men, under Captain Fitzpatrick, had been cut off by the Indians at Pague River, and all most inhumanly murdered. A man named Lewis Pollock was called from his bed on the night of the great fire and shot dead by a man named Samuel Gallagher. The citizens of Marysville had formed a vigilant committee for the protection of their lives and property. The accounts from the mines and placers were very favorable, and the prospects of the crops throughout the country were very encouraging. San Francisco is being rebuilt very rapidly, notwithstanding her sad reverses. Two hundred buildings have been erected during the past week. HORRIBLE MURDER AT SONORA.—A most shocking and horrible murder has been perpetrated at Sonora, the details of which are seldom equaled. Some persons who had taken offense at an article which appeared in the Sonora Herald, went to the room of the editor, Dr. Gunn, dragged him from his bed, and deliberately shot him through the head. He died instantly. They also murdered two other persons connected with the same office and killed or wounded some three or four others who went to their assistance. This affair has produced the most intense excitement. California shipments continue large, and far beyond actual wants. DEATHS IN SAN FRANCISCO.—Died in San Francisco, June 11, Thomas Lansdown, of Chicago, aged 26; P. X. Curry, of Wisconsin, aged 30. On the 10th, Aaron Sands, of Philadelphia, aged 37 years. On the 6th, Richard McFarland, of Baltimore. THE MARKETS.—Previous to the fire there was an improved demand for all kinds of goods. The fire, however, has tended much to unsettle the market, but there still remains a fair demand from the interior. The supply of breadstuffs is large. Bricks are in fair request at $30 for common to $50 per 1,000 for fine. Coal is dull at $14.

spellchecked: THE LYNCH LAW EXECUTERS IN CALIFORNIA. It is to the New York Commercial Advertiser. It will be remembered that when first the intelligence reached us that a so-called "vigilance committee" had been formed at San Francisco on Lynch-law principles, and that, instead of endeavoring to make the courts purer and more efficient, the committee assumed to be independent of and superior to the law and its officers, we deprecated the whole movement as containing the very essence of anarchy and misrule, as in fact substituting violence and an irresponsible authority for recognized institutions with officers amenable to the people. We saw in that step the introduction of a principle that sooner or later must work mischief—for principles are indestructible and operative, and must produce results. The emergency of the case was pressed upon us, and we were told that in no other way could life and property be protected; that the committee were all honorable; that the popular sentiment was entirely with them—a fact which was undoubtedly true at one time, but now proved untrue, as shown by the hideous longing for an exception evinced by the populace when Whitaker and McKenzie hung. The ground assumed in these columns with reference to the vigilance committee system was, that it was wrong in principle, and therefore eventually become evil in practice; that the assumption of authority vested elsewhere by the people, and by them legitimately transferred to the vigilance committee; that it was not merely a local Patton of magical and executive power, but a violent opposition to the laws and constitution of the State, a despotic administration of life and death, of unheard-of punishments, and of "Star Chamber" examinations and convictions—all tending to demoralize and debase the people, by making them familiar with summary convictions and executions without the show of mercy and forbearance or decent ceremony. The last narrative that we published of one of these executions was truly horrifying, and more than justified our censures and prophecies. Its effect upon the community, as described by an independent writer (a citizen of San Francisco) "Two of the vigilance committee have alienated from them some of their best friends, as well as a large majority of this community. You have already heard of the execution by this committee of Whitaker and McKenzie on Sunday. Suffice it to say that that horrid deed has so shocked this community that confidence in the humanity and prudence of the committees has yet to be restored. This community contends if they were so wanting in vigilance as to permit the authorities to take the prisoners from them, they should have let them pass and determined to be careful in future; but this breaking into the prison, and in a spirit of retaliation upon the authorities, hanging these guilty men on Sunday is an outrage which the better part of the community cannot be made either to sanction or tolerate. This committee will hereafter only be commended for any lawful efforts which they may use in bringing criminals to justice, but the time is past when this community will permit them to become judges and executioners." Another move which has already rendered the committee unpopular is an effort on the part of many of its leading men to get up what they have called a land monopoly ticket at the elections. This has caused some to believe that the extensive land claimants and wealthy will in some way or other use this vigilance committee to favor their own selfish ends. We do not know whether these fears are groundless or otherwise, but the truth is the committee no longer has the bone and sinew of this community with it, and it is safe to infer that no executions will again be made by its authority. That the vigilance committee is losing the confidence of leading men, and becoming the subject of suspicion and vituperation, is not to be wondered at. The only marvel is that such despotic and dangerous power has been permitted to establish itself upon its present basis. But what will follow this reaction of public sentiment? Will the members of the committee themselves be safe from reprisals? May the same people who delighted when the committee took prisoners from the city jail and gave an exhibition of a double execution on the Sabbath, may this populace take its second thought and join the authorities in demanding from the committee the evidence of its legal right to condemn and hang for crimes which the constitution does not punish with death? And how is the committee prepared for such a day of reckoning? It is one thing to suspend a man from a beam and jerk him up and down until he is killed, as in the above Sunday execution, amid the howlings of a gratified mob, and it is another and widely different thing to face a stern, properly constituted, legal tribunal which, by the silent but unceasing operation of a great principle, has recovered its authority with the people, and can now punish those who assumed its powers and exercised, and even exceeded, its prerogatives.

spellchecked: Our Journal, and forwarded through Adams & Co. or Gregory's Express, will be attended to without delay. Lynch Law—Three Indians Executed. Judge Lynch has recently been holding his session in the western part of our county. He has pursued quite a different course in his official career to that of his contemporaries, and sometimes, perhaps not unjustly; though we hope the time has passed, when it can be said such things are necessary for the protection of the lives and property of our citizens, except in extreme cases. The hindrance has been, when it was almost impossible, in consequence of the growing character of our population, to convict a man of any crime by the regular courts of justice, it being impossible to obtain witnesses. But another consideration once combined with this to excite these summary calls of justice. We were assembled from all parts of the world, strangers, and almost unknown to each other, and unless a villain were apprehended and executed himself in the act of his crime, his identity could scarcely be proven in after time. But these and other excuses for such summary proceedings are fast vanishing before the rapid improvements of our society. And it were better to bear with a little evil in the tardy workings of judicial operations, than to risk the great liability of an excited multitude doing injustice to innocent persons suspected of crime. No one will doubt the correctness of the intentions of those engaging in those summary executions; but all who have observed their operations in California for the last two years must have observed their great liability to err, and the difficulty with which their excited tempers can be controlled when once public feeling has set in against an individual. Some two or three weeks since, two men named Ross and Pope were apprehended at Newtown for stealing, and not being able to get evidence enough even to have them bound over for trial, one of them was sentenced to be hung, for the avowed purpose of making him confess the crime, but through the timely interference of Messrs. McConnell, Endicott, and others, he was rescued. On Monday last, another man was arrested for stealing; in which case we do not know the character of the evidence; but he was sentenced to receive a few lashes, which sentence was duly executed. In addition to those, we have received the following communication—the detail of another execution: "At a court held on the 1st day of June, 1852, at Wilson's ranch, by the inhabitants residing in the vicinity, for the trial of Yalla, Leno, Camerock, and Hoosppa, four Indians charged with the murder of Martin Hopkins, on the 1st day of June, 1852. On motion, K. McDowell was appointed Judge, James C. Murdoch Clerk, O. Evans attorney for the people, and Samuel S. Gentilins counsel for the prisoners. The following persons, to wit: C. C. Williams, A. G. Cole, J. J. Runks, Wm. H. Knowles, C. Musgrove, Geo. Baller, Jas. Rathbun, L. P. Poor, W. X. Farber, and N. S. Chaplin, were sworn and empaneled a jury for the trial of the prisoners, who, having heard the evidence—as well on the part of the people as the prisoners—retired a short distance, and after some time returned with the following verdict: "We, the jury, find the defendants Yalla, Leno, and Hocapa guilty, and adjudge that they be at once executed by hanging. No evidence being adduced against the defendant Camerock, we therefore find him not guilty." We do not sit in judgment to condemn the acts of this court and jury. The sentence, we are informed, was duly executed. The trial and execution was done all upon the instant, without giving the mind that time necessary to sober down after an excitement, and look at the circumstances with an unprejudiced eye. The man who will never form unjust conclusions in this way, approximates perfection to a degree not allowed to the great body of human beings; for we are all creatures of passion and prejudices, and he who will never act is almost invariably hasty.

ELOPEMENT AND LYNCH LAW.—A white girl, aged about 17 or 18, of respectable parentage, eloped from Frederick County, last week, with a rough, rude, overgrown black fellow. On Saturday night, at a late hour, they arrived in Hagerstown on their way for Pennsylvania, and were arrested by our vigilant police officers. The black fellow was committed to jail and the deluded girl taken care of until Monday morning, when the man was taken before one of our magistrates; but having committed no offense, as it was thought, for which the law provided a punishment, he was about being dismissed, when the mob manifested a disposition to take him in hand. A commitment was then made out for the purpose of placing him in jail beyond the reach of the mob, and he was given over to the peace officers; but on the way to the jail, the indignant crowd seized him, and placing him on a rail, rushed forward with the intention of passing the jail gate. The officers who had him in charge, however, with great exertions and much to their credit, succeeded in directing the course of the mob into the gate, and thus got their charge within the prison yard. Here a parley took place which resulted in a compromise, according to which the offender received thirty-nine stripes on the bare back, well laid on. He was then committed; and in the afternoon, escorted out of town by a committee appointed to keep off the mob, and permitted to pursue his way for Pennsylvania.

spellchecked: MURDER AND LYNCHING AT THE WEST.—We copy from the Chicago (Illinois) American the following particulars respecting the murder of a Mr. Campbell, on Rock River, and the occurrences that subsequently took place. The country below this and north of the Illinois River has been for a long time and is now infested with a gang of blacklegs, counterfeiters, horse thieves and land pirates, and the good people have found our laws, or at least the administration of them, entirely inadequate to the protection of their property. Consequently, they have been forced to form themselves into "volunteer companies and anti-horse thief societies." One was formed about 20 miles below this, at Washington Grove. Mr. Campbell was actively engaged in such efforts when, in June, two of the Driskells, notorious throughout this region as ringleaders and harborers of all sorts of villains, rode up to Campbell's house and asked his son if his father was at home. He called his father to the door, when the Driskells shot him dead, and fled. The volunteer companies of DeKalb and Winnebago Counties immediately collected and went in search of the Driskells. On Tuesday they caught the old man and one of his sons; tried them by Lynch law, and were convinced that they were the cause, if not the perpetrators, of the atrocious murder of Mr. Campbell. They sentenced them to immediate death, then placed the old man about ten rods off, and bade him prepare for death, giving him 5 minutes. When the time was up, about 50 balls went through him. The son was then served in the same manner—both devils proving game—neither making any disclosures, more than saying that another son had killed Campbell. The companies are now pursuing this other Driskell, who has cut stick with a confederate. $500 reward is offered for his head. High-handed and revolting as this summary mode of procedure seems to be, it is, nevertheless, absolutely necessary, and receives the commendation of every individual who is at all acquainted with the facts. If a man refuses to join these companies, he is at once put down with the horse thieves.

A friend of ours, who arrived in the city yesterday, informs us of the manner in which that law—more tyrannical than the code of Draco—Lynch Law—has, in this as well as in every other instance where it has been appealed to, been carried into effect. Between the 5th and 10th inst., Phillips County, in Arkansas, about 40 miles below Helena, and the County of Coahoma, in Mississippi, on the opposite side of the river, appear to have become the scene of mob and lynch law to a greater extent than has lately been recorded by the public press. A numerous gang of counterfeiters had their places of rendezvous and the abodes of their families in the above-named counties, to the great and continued annoyance of the citizens and the trading flatboatmen on the river. Besides their encroachment on the peace and property of the public in that way, they of late turned their criminal industry to horse stealing to such an extent as to rouse the citizens of the whole neighborhood. The latter, headed by Capt. Barney Bradford, formed into a volunteer company of about 100 well-armed men, commanded and led by said Capt. Bradford, Mr. J. Lunsford, and Spear (from Arkansas), and Squire Forrer and James Howarton (from Mississippi), and after an active search of several days, succeeded in capturing 27 men, among whom we learned the following names, viz: Hugh Tally, Lewis Hingston, Andrew McLaughlin, Willis Pollock, Hugh Cotton, Elliot and Robert Hunter (the latter, lately from New York), Joe Merritt and McCormick. The volunteers used the following stratagem to seize the scoundrels. They engaged a trading flatboat at Helena and hid about 50 men in the storeroom; then they descended the river, landing at a place where they suspected to fall in with the counterfeiters. These depraved men came on board with the intention to purchase produce, paying for it in counterfeit money. They were thus taken and secured in the boat. When the number had increased to 27 men, nine of them were tied hand and feet, and, as the report says, drowned in the Mississippi, near Island No. 69, in the presence of two men, Harrod and Burgess, who, it appears, officiated, or at least took an active part in the execution of the sentence. We understood that the company is increasing in number, and intends to proceed to the mouth of White River. When our informant met a division of them they were in pursuit of a certain Meriwether Wright. When he arrived at Napoleon, at the mouth of Arkansas River, he learned that some six or seven dead bodies had been seen floating on the river opposite that place, and also that some of the counterfeiters who escaped had been seen passing down the river with uncommon speed, in order to evade their pursuers.—Picayune.

spellchecked: ILLINOIS LYNCH LAW.—Since our account of last week, with regard to the lynching tragedy in Ogle County, Illinois, we have received conflicting and contradictory statements through the papers, of the circumstances connected with that transaction.—From all that we are able to learn, it would seem the more prudent portion of the people are far from justifying the summary trial and execution of the two Driskells, for the alleged murder of John Campbell. A Coroner's inquest has been held upon the bodies of the Driskells, and the jury have returned a verdict of willful murder! This then, is likely to result in serious business to those who assumed to take the law into their own hands. We learn that immediately after the mob had wreaked their vengeance upon the lives of two Driskells, they repaired to the residences of all the Driskells and expelled the widowed and orphaned families, and burnt their houses to the ground. It is also stated that money and valuable papers were upon the persons of the Driskells at the time of their being shot, which were abstracted from their pockets by the mob. The Driskells were the owners of valuable farms, which are under a high state of cultivation, and covered with extensive crops of growing grain. The mob have forbidden, under the penalty of death, any persons from harvesting the crops. Bridge, whom we stated last week as being one of the murderers of Campbell, has been arrested, tried, and acquitted. We learn from the Galena papers that the office of the "Rockford Star" was entered by the mob on the night of the 6th instant, and the type and fixtures so much injured and mutilated that the paper has been obliged to discontinue. The alleged cause for this transaction is that the Star has spoken out in condemnation of the proceedings of the mob. In a good government, Lynch Law can never be justified. Lynch Law is the stepping stone to anarchy, misrule, and uncontrollable violence. To say that the laws of the States are inadequate to perform the demands of human justice is a libel upon our government and institutions. It is a foul charge, which the enemies of republicanism in Europe have ever attempted to fasten upon us, but one which we in theory have ever repudiated and denied. The lynchers of the Driskells plead in justification that the friends of good order were too weak to enforce the law, and bring the offenders to merited justice.—This cannot be true. The same power which was brought into requisition to bring the Driskells before a lynch tribunal, was amply adequate to have brought them before a legal court of the State of Illinois. The laws of Illinois for the apprehension, conviction, and punishment of felons and murderers, are as speedy and as rigid as in any other State in the Union.

spellchecked: LYNCH LAW. Lynch law is a law of blood. Its decisions, in some instances, have a show of justice to slightly palliate its deeds of murder. But at the recent outbreak in Kentucky, we are shocked beyond measure. It is the most unwarrantable act that has ever been perpetrated in the name of a bloody monster. Let no man talk to us of the respectability of some of the parties concerned. They have the blood of the murdered men in their skirts. The great rivers of the West are not sufficient to wash away the stain. Nor can the fertile land obscure the scent of blood or the fragrant flowers that will go with them to their graves. The public press, the many-mouthed press that speaks for the whole nation, a press that is bound to keep our escutcheon as a people unsullied, should issue, one and all, its anathemas against this damning deed. It will plant in many a thoughtless heart that entered this bloody list without reflection, a pang that time can never remove. We would not, for all the wealth of every man concerned in the assault, have the thought upon our dying pillow that we weakly, remotely helped in this deed of infamy. We take this resolute stand that we may set men to thinking. The public mind and public morals must be kept up to a standard that will not allow a man rashly to take the vengeance of the laws in his own hands. The blush of shame may not mantle offense upon a Lyncher's cheek when he perpetrates it, but in due season the whips of conscience will lash him most severely when he may seek most fervently for repose. They have not only wronged their country, but themselves and their children. Other lynchers may long lie in wait for them.—[American Sentinel.]

spellchecked: RIOT IN CINCINNATI, OHIO. A Letter to the editors of the New York New Era, from Cincinnati, Ohio, dated the 4th inst., gives an account of a very serious riot in that city. On the evening of the 2d, a quarrel occurred between several negroes and two white men, in which the latter were badly wounded with dirk knives. About 9 o'clock on the following evening, a large concourse of people, without concert or arms, assembled in the immediate vicinity of "Five Points," or, as it is called, "Nigger Town." A few persons in the mob, which consisted of 3 or 400, threw stones against the buildings of the negroes. The negroes immediately poured into the mob a volley of bullets, from muskets and rifles, with which they had previously provided themselves in anticipation of an attack. The mob, being unarmed, fled precipitately, and were pursued for nearly a square by the blacks, who yelled out a wild shout of triumph and defiance, and returned to their houses. About midnight the mob advanced to the position they had occupied in the early part of the evening, provided with arms and a six-pounder. The six-pounder and small arms were fired, which was returned by the blacks, and the parties engaged in a terrible conflict. Fortunately for the lives of many, the prompt arrival of the military silenced the firing, restored peace, and dispersed the mob. There are various reports of the number killed and wounded on both sides, the truth of which cannot at present be known. The city was all in confusion and uproar again on the 4th, and the negroes flying in all directions. There was no fighting or lynching, but the people were taking the negroes into custody as fast as they could be caught, with the design of enforcing a law which requires all colored residents of Ohio to give bond for their good behavior or leave the State.

We have been put in possession of the facts in relation to this affair, which is one among the last Texas tragedies. Cattle had been stolen, robberies committed, and citizens insulted and murdered; but still, whenever any were arrested on the charge, the gang came forward with perjured oaths, and they were acquitted. "Yoakum" was hardened into the most inveterate degree of crime, and seemed but to reap enjoyment by pursuing the most fiendish acts of robbery and murder. It is a most singular instance of the effects of habit. He was a rich and affluent planter, and lived in a sumptuous and most magnificent manner—kept a splendid equipage—owned over a hundred negroes and large tracts of land—had constantly about a hundred breeding mares, made a yearly sale of fifteen hundred cattle, and had a large revenue coming from other sources. There is no doubt that he was the richest man in Texas. Yet with all this wealth, his disposition to plunder knew no bounds. The cause of his death arose from an abortive attempt to murder Mr. Carey of Houston County.—Mr. C. is a highly respectable and wealthy citizen of the town of Houston, and was at the time staying at the residence of Yoakum. He was suspected of having a large sum of money with him, and Yoakum determined that he should be murdered while in bed. The plan was properly managed during the day, and everything placed in readiness for the commission. Nothing remained but the darkness of the night.
